summary: Specifies how to use SIP to establish an SRTP security context using DTLS. It describes carrying a fingerprint attribute in SDP to bind the signaling to the DTLS handshake used on the media path. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5763 explains how SIP endpoints can set up SRTP keys through a DTLS handshake on the media path. Each endpoint checks the certificate received in that handshake against a fingerprint carried in SDP signaling.

subtitle: How SIP endpoints bind a DTLS media handshake to the fingerprints carried in SDP.

tldr.problem: SIP endpoints need to establish secure media without placing media keys in signaling or requiring every endpoint to have a certificate from a well-known authority.
tldr.mechanism: Each endpoint places a certificate fingerprint in its SDP offer or answer. The endpoints establish a mutually authenticated DTLS connection on the media path and compare the presented certificates with those fingerprints.
tldr.outcome: The keys are negotiated between media endpoints, while signaling binds the handshake to the call. Protection against active attacks depends on signaling integrity. RFC 5763 is updated by RFC 8842.

today: RFC 5763 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010 and is updated by RFC 8842.

sections.title: Binding Media Security to SIP Signaling
sections.content:
SIP and SDP set up calls, while RTP carries real-time media. RFC 5763 describes how endpoints establish SRTP security using DTLS. The key exchange travels on the media path, and the SIP/SDP offer and answer carry fingerprints that identify the certificates used in the DTLS handshake.

Certificates can be self-signed because the fingerprint links each certificate to the signaling. The endpoints do not need certificates signed by a well-known authority, but they do need a way to protect the integrity of the signaling carrying those fingerprints.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints exchange certificate fingerprints in call signaling, then establish media keys using DTLS. Each side checks that the certificate on the media connection matches the fingerprint it received.

sections.title: How the Fingerprint Check Works
sections.content:
An offerer sends an SDP offer with its certificate fingerprint. The answerer and offerer establish a mutually authenticated DTLS connection on the media path. Each endpoint compares the certificate from the handshake with the fingerprint in the corresponding SDP offer or answer.

The fingerprint protects against an attacker who changes only the media connection. It does not by itself protect against an attacker who can change the signaling. SIP Identity or another integrity mechanism can protect the fingerprint while it travels through proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint in the call description identifies the certificate expected during the media handshake. If the certificate does not match, the endpoint must end the media session.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Requirements
sections.content:
The offerer uses setup:actpass and must be ready to receive a DTLS ClientHello before the answer arrives. The answerer uses setup:active or setup:passive; active is recommended because the handshake can run alongside the answer.

Endpoints use the certificate fingerprint attribute defined for SDP and do not use the connection attribute from RFC 4145. The certificate in the DTLS handshake must match the fingerprint in signaling. If it does not match, the endpoint must immediately tear down the media session.
sections.plainLanguage: The offerer says it can take either DTLS role. The answerer selects a role, and both endpoints must check the handshake certificate against the SDP fingerprint.

sections.title: Early Media, Forking, and Rekeying
sections.content:
The active endpoint starts the DTLS handshake. An endpoint sending early media must take the active role, though the other side may not yet have validated its certificate fingerprint. When a request forks to several endpoints, each answerer establishes a separate DTLS association with the offerer.

Endpoints can reuse compatible associations during session changes or establish a new association. They can rekey by running another DTLS handshake while continuing to use the existing keys until the new keys are ready. If the active and passive roles change, a new connection is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint that answers a forked call establishes its own secure media association. During rekeying, the call can keep using the existing keys until replacement keys are ready.

sections.title: Signaling Integrity and Peer Identity
sections.content:
The security of the media handshake depends on the integrity of the fingerprint in signaling. If an attacker can change both signaling and media traffic, the attacker may replace the fingerprint and interfere with the connection. SIP Identity can sign the offer; RFC 4916 describes a way for the answerer to send its identity in a signed follow-up request.

Without signaling integrity, the mechanism mainly protects against passive observers. A privacy-focused call may also need a fresh self-signed certificate to reduce correlation between calls. RFC 5763 is updated by RFC 8842.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is useful only if an attacker cannot replace it in signaling. Endpoints need an integrity-protected signaling method to link the media certificate to the intended peer.

messages.label: DTLS handshake on media path
messages.note: The certificate is checked against the SDP fingerprint.
